source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) matched or beat college students on Digit Matrices (new text matrix task) and verbal analogies, zero-shot.
numbers: Digit Matrices, humans N=40: GPT-3 generative OR=1.88 (p=0.005, CI 1.21-2.91); multiple choice OR=6.27 (p=2.3e-8). Verbal analogy sets: SAT items above estimated high-school average; humans N=57 (UCLA VAT), N=20, N=241.
limits: Overlap with training data argued away by the authors only; later counterfactual studies (c03, c04) dispute generality.
agent_relevance: Shows the model can pick out relational structure. This is the positive-analogy step, not yet the strength-of-argument step.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models (story analogies, causal)
finding: Test close to Hesse's causal condition: pick the target story that shares the source's causal relations. Humans clearly beat GPT-3 on far (cross-domain) analogies.
numbers: Humans N=54: t(53)=21.3 overall; 15/54 chose the analogous story on every trial. GPT-3 above chance in near (p=0.0039) but not far (p=0.065). Human vs GPT-3 OR=0.37 (p=0.0003, CI 0.21-0.63). GPT-4 preliminary: better, near-perfect on near.
limits: Items from Gentner et al. story sets; GPT-4 tested only informally (supplement S4.3).
agent_relevance: The causal-link check is a weak spot for models in cross-domain cases, so a code-checked causal-link guardrail should not rely on the model's own judgement of causal match.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Re-ran Webb's letter-string analogies with permuted or symbol alphabets. GPT-3, 3.5, 4 dropped sharply; humans stayed high. Failed generality replication.
numbers: Humans stayed high on all variants; all three GPT models fell on counterfactual alphabets. Share of errors that used an alternate valid rule: GPT-3.5 38.59%, GPT-4 22%, GPT-3 5.81%; humans about 15% (read from error table).
limits: Small item sets; Prolific humans; chat tuning may hurt (authors' own caveat). Webb et al. 2024 (c05) answer this.
agent_relevance: Argument strength must be tested on counterfactual or renamed instances (fits G3: pass on something not fitted).

source: Hodel & West (2023) Response: Emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Cited by Webb 2024 and Stevenson 2025: GPT-3 and GPT-4 degrade on permuted-alphabet, larger-interval letter-string variants. Not opened by me; known only via citing papers.
numbers: Numbers not read.
limits: Second-hand only.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as c03.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2024) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Reply: Digit Matrices already used counterfactual reordering of digits 1-9, and GPT-3 beat humans there. GPT-4 with code execution handles the counterfactual letter-string items; its errors look like human ones.
numbers: GPT-4 + code execution vs humans: P=0.496 (no difference); GPT-4 alone below humans. 46% (23/50) of GPT-4 errors used a valid alternate rule vs 39% of human errors in the Lewis & Mitchell data.
limits: Authors of the original claim; code execution is a scaffold, not the bare model.
agent_relevance: A code tool restores performance: supports putting rule checks in code (G5) rather than in model judgement.

source: Musker, Duchnowski, Milliere, Pavlick (2025) LLMs as models for analogical reasoning, J. Memory & Language 145
finding: New tasks mapping meaningful words to letter or symbol sequences (semantic structure, semantic content). Advanced LLMs match humans in several conditions but react differently to distractors and task variations.
numbers: Per-condition table values not extracted. Paper notes individual human subjects ranged from 50% to 100% match in the Distracted condition.
limits: Authors conclude LLMs give a how-possibly, not how-actually, account of human analogy.
agent_relevance: Surface-similar distractors are exactly the essential-difference-under-similarity case; test with distractors.

source: Sourati et al. (2024) ARN: Analogical Reasoning on Narratives
finding: Benchmark separating surface from system (relational) mappings in narratives. Models do fine on near analogies and fail on far ones; GPT-4 is below chance on far analogies zero-shot.
numbers: Humans 94.1% on far analogies vs models 39.6% average (chance 50%). Near analogies: humans 97.9%, models 75.0%. (far,far) 45.3%; far analogy vs near distractor 33.9%; near analogy vs far disanalogy 76.9%. GPT-4 best, average 68.1%; SBERT 42.3% (1% when a far analogy must win).
limits: Binary choice; zero-shot prompts that told models to prefer system mappings did not help.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that models are lured by surface similarity over relational (causal) match. A guardrail should compare relational structure by code and flag similarity-only matches.

source: Sourati et al. (2024) ARN: few-shot and chain-of-thought demonstrations
finding: Few-shot demonstrations with chain-of-thought rationales raised accuracy, but the best model still sat about halfway between random and humans.
numbers: Exact few-shot figures not extracted; the abstract states the best model is halfway between random and humans in the few-shot setting.
limits: Near-analogy demonstrations help less on far analogies (paper note).
agent_relevance: A scaffold that makes the model state the mapping step by step helps some, but does not close the gap.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024, ICLR) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Analogical prompting: the model writes its own relevant example problems (and optional tutorial) before solving. Beat 0-shot CoT and often manual few-shot CoT.
numbers: Average gain about +4% (intro). Diverse vs non-diverse exemplars: GSM8K 77.8 vs 75.9; MATH 37.3 vs 35.2 (GPT-3.5-turbo). With self-consistency: GSM8K 85.3, MATH 46.0. Codeforces GPT-3.5 Acc@1 about 15% with knowledge+exemplars vs 8-9% for baselines. Gains larger with bigger models; retrieved CoT better with small models.
limits: Some table rows are garbled in extracted text; only pairable figures quoted. No check on the quality of the analogue.
agent_relevance: This is a source-selection step with no Hesse or Bartha check. It is the main in-loop use of analogy, and c10 shows it may not rest on relevance.

source: Qin et al. (2025) Relevant or Random: Can LLMs truly perform analogical reasoning?
finding: Failed replication of the mechanism. Self-generated irrelevant (random) examples do as well or better than relevant ones on math. The accuracy of the generated examples, not their relevance, matters.
numbers: GSM8K/MATH (GPT-3.5): all random-example types beat relevant ones; random biological examples about +2.5% over relevant math examples; no-example baseline best on average; up to 4% gain on GSM8K with random biology. BBH average: Relevant 63.2, Random-same 61.9, Random-bio 60.4, Random-diff 56.4 (relevance helps there, +1.3%). Accuracy of generated examples: Relevant 62%, none 72%, Random-same 86%. Similarity to query: relevant 0.48 vs oracle 0.64.
limits: GPT-3.5 mainly; GPT-4o-mini in appendix; temperature 0; three seeds.
agent_relevance: Strong warning: analogy in prompts may help for reasons other than analogy. Checking the correctness of the source (by code) matters more than similarity.

source: Qin et al. (2025) Relevant or Random: accuracy-based fixes
finding: Two cheaper methods built from the finding; GPT-4 calibration of examples beat plain in-context analogical prompting, random examples were worst.
numbers: Table 7: GPT4-Calibration consistently better than ICL; random always worst. Exact deltas not extracted.
limits: Uses a stronger model to check weaker model's examples.
agent_relevance: Matches G2/G3: verify the source analogue with a real check before borrowing from it.

source: Stevenson et al. (2025) Can LLMs generalize analogy solving like children can?
finding: Letter-string analogies in Latin, Greek (near transfer) and symbol list (far transfer). Children (7-9) and adults transferred; LLMs did not.
limits: Chat models; one task type.
agent_relevance: Even child-level transfer fails once the surface changes: the surface-vs-structure split is the core risk for argument by analogy.

source: Opielka, Rosenbusch, Stevenson (2025) Analogical reasoning inside LLMs: concept vectors and the limits of abstraction
finding: Inside the model, function vectors change with surface form, but a few attention heads hold concept vectors that are invariant for antonym and category. No invariant vector for abstract concepts like previous/next.
numbers: Llama-3.1 70B, 600 ICL prompts. Reported figures include 58% vs 2% in one steering comparison and 98% accuracy for previous/next with ordered lists vs 62% for abstract previous/next.
limits: Mechanistic study, small task set, open models only.
agent_relevance: The model can hold a correct inner concept and still give a wrong output, so an external check on the final mapping is needed.

source: Lampinen et al. (2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: Models, like humans, reason better when meaning supports the logical inference (syllogisms, NLI, Wason). Belief bias applies to models.
numbers: Text cites humans mistakenly accepting believable-but-invalid syllogisms about 90% of the time (earlier work) and maths majors under 50% on a Wason variant.
limits: Not analogy; relevant because a plausible target conclusion can pass an unsound argument.
agent_relevance: Plausibility of the conclusion will bias the model's verdict on analogical strength. Mask the conclusion when judging the mapping.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large language models can be easily distracted by irrelevant context (GSM-IC)
finding: One irrelevant sentence added to a problem sharply cuts accuracy. Self-consistency and an instruction to ignore irrelevant information help.
numbers: With 20 samples the correct answer appears somewhere in 99.7% of GSM-IC problems (recall). Instruction added to CoT raised one split from 73.5 to 79.0.
limits: Arithmetic, not analogy.
agent_relevance: A critical disanalogy often hides as irrelevant-looking detail; models are weak at ignoring or weighing it. Use code to list differences explicitly.

source: Yu, He, Ying (2024, ICLR) Thought Propagation: an analogical approach to complex reasoning
finding: LLM proposes and solves analogous problems, then reuses their solutions or plans to amend its first answer. Works inside agent loops.
numbers: Average +12% absolute in finding optimal shortest paths, +13% human preference in Creative Writing, +15% task completion in ALFWorld agent planning (134 tasks).
limits: No criterion for when an analogue is good; relies on the model's own proposal.
agent_relevance: An existing agent-loop use of analogy. A Hesse/Bartha-style check would be a filter on which analogues to propagate from.

source: Hu, Storks, Lewis, Chai (2023) In-context analogical reasoning with pre-trained language models
finding: Raven's matrices encoded as language: pre-trained LMs reach above-human zero-shot accuracy; higher-level abstractions of features helped more.
numbers: OPT 125M accuracy rose from 22.2% to 45.6% in one encoding comparison; best Center sub-task accuracy up to 95.6% (table labels partly garbled).
limits: Perceptual features supplied by hand-coded text.
agent_relevance: Giving the relational structure in words helps mapping: supports having code extract and present relations.

source: Bartha (2019) Analogy and Analogical Reasoning, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
finding: Hesse's three conditions: material similarity (horizontal), causal vertical relations in the source, and no essential difference (no key source property in the negative analogy). Bartha 2010 replaces them with Prior Association and Potential for Generalization (no critical disanalogy).
numbers: Qualitative only. About the first 100,000 of 135,000 characters were read through a summariser; the V1/V2/H1/H2 labels did not appear in it.
limits: Hesse's causal condition is too restrictive for some maths analogies (SEP). Modal vs probabilistic readings of plausibility.
agent_relevance: These are the testable parts: causal link in the source, a list of differences, and a check that none touches the causal link.

source: Bartha (2010) By Parallel Reasoning, OUP
finding: Source of the articulation model. Not opened; described via SEP.
numbers: None.
limits: Not read.
agent_relevance: Formal basis for a code-checkable two-part rule.

source: Hesse (1966) Models and Analogies in Science, Notre Dame
finding: Source of the material criteria; positive, negative and neutral analogy terms come from Keynes 1921 (per SEP).
numbers: None.
limits: Not read.
agent_relevance: Keynes terms give a data structure: three lists per case.

source: Davies & Russell (1987) A logical approach to reasoning by analogy, IJCAI-87
finding: Older AI system: analogy as valid inference when a determination rule says the shared features fix the projected feature. Known only from the SEP bibliography and my background; not opened.
numbers: None.
limits: Content not read here.
agent_relevance: Closest formal ancestor of a causal link as a code test: a determination rule is a checkable object.

source: Search finding: LLM tests of Hesse or Bartha criteria
finding: No paper found that tests language models on Hesse's material criteria or Bartha's articulation model directly. Closest: Gentner-style causal vs surface choices (c02, c07) and relevance tests (c10).
numbers: arXiv listing and OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar were rate-limited; direct paper checks only. Zero direct hits.
limits: Absence under a rate-limited search is not proof; legal-reasoning LLM papers may exist.
agent_relevance: Open gap: a Hesse/Bartha guardrail would be new, so its effect must be measured by us.

source: Mitchell (2021) Abstraction and analogy-making in AI
finding: Cited by Lewis & Mitchell and Stevenson 2025 as the frame for testing transfer. Not opened.
numbers: None.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Supports counterfactual testing.

source: Stevenson et al. (2025) item analysis
finding: Rule type matters: items with a predecessor rule were hardest for both children and LLMs; a separate task checked that models knew next/previous letters.
numbers: Item 5 (predecessor + repetition) worst; item 1 (successor only) best; Next-Previous Letter Task built as the knowledge check.
limits: Five items per alphabet.
agent_relevance: Check that the model knows the component relations before blaming the mapping.

source: Webb et al. (2023) letter strings to real-world concepts
finding: Letter strings mapped to real-world concepts (e.g. p q r : p q s :: cold cool warm : ?) were solved zero-shot; Webb 2024 cites this as novel material unlikely to be on the internet.
numbers: Per-condition percentages not extracted here.
limits: Source of the contested claim.
agent_relevance: Cross-domain mapping works for simple relations; strength for rich causal systems is untested.

source: Gentner & Toupin (1986) systematicity and transfer (cited in Webb 2023, Sourati 2024)
finding: Human baseline: systematic (causal) similarity beats surface similarity, and children rely more on surface. Cited only; not opened.
numbers: None extracted.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Human baseline that ARN and Webb story analogies reproduce for models.
